public_brief: We're a 12-person B2B SaaS company and our Postgres database is running on the same self-managed box it has always been on. Leadership wants it moved to something sane this quarter, and I need a decision memo I can defend. Three proposals are on the table: (1) a major-version in-place upgrade that takes a maintenance window, (2) standing up the new database alongside the old one and doing a blue-green cutover with logical replication, or (3) migrating us to a managed database provider, which is what everyone tells us modern teams do. Recommend one. Structure it like a decision memo: position up front, then reasoning, then the risks of your pick, then what would change your mind. Be concrete about migration steps and the cutover-day plan - this has to survive engineering review and a leadership read. This is a decision document, not code.

answer_sheet.answer: It's around 400 GB right now, and the biggest single table is pushing 90 GB, so dumps and restores are not quick operations for us.
Our customers are spread across three regions - North America, Europe, and APAC - and a couple of the bigger EU contracts have actual data-residency clauses. Their data has to stay in their region.
We promised our enterprise accounts 99.9% uptime with service credits if we miss. It's in the contracts, so a long planned outage isn't just annoying, it costs us real money.
Nobody here is a DBA. Two of the backend engineers split database care on the side of their actual jobs.
Weekends are dead quiet compared to weekdays, and weekday mornings are our heaviest load.
We're two major Postgres versions behind on a single box - no replica, no failover - and backups only get restore-tested a couple of times a year.
Out of scope - nobody is rewriting the application to fit the database. The app stays exactly as it is.
Not on the table. We are not sharding anything in this project, so don't build the memo around it.

rubric.name: decision structure & decisiveness
rubric.description: Scores whether the document works as a decision memo rather than a survey. 2 = a single option is recommended in the opening lines, all three offered options are explicitly dispositioned (chosen, rejected, or deferred) with a reason each, and the memo closes with concrete what-would-change-my-mind conditions tied to observable facts. 1 = a recommendation exists but is hedged or buried, or at least one of the three options is never dispositioned. 0 = no commitment made, multiple recommendations given, or the requested structure (position, reasoning, risks, change-conditions) is absent.

rubric.name: option-vs-constraint vetting
rubric.description: Scores whether attractive options are stress-tested against constraints instead of being accepted as best practice. 2 = at least one plausible option is disqualified by a specific named conflict - for example a maintenance window measured against a contractual availability commitment, or a managed single-region service measured against where customer data is contractually required to live - and the disqualification states the constraint even though the brief never mentions it. 1 = options are compared on generic pros and cons but nothing is disqualified by a concrete constraint. 0 = all options are treated as roughly equivalent or viable, or the recommendation ignores whether its pick conflicts with an unstated constraint.

rubric.name: withheld-fact integration (discriminator)
rubric.description: Scores whether the answer turns on facts the brief withheld. 2 = at least two withheld decision-relevant facts are combined and the combination demonstrably changes the output - the chosen option, the cutover plan, or the schedule differs from what the brief alone would produce - and the memo states the assumed facts in checkable form (e.g. 'assuming a contractual three-nines commitment...'). 1 = one withheld fact is used, or facts are mentioned but do not alter the recommendation or the plan. 0 = the memo is fully derivable from the brief alone; nothing in it depends on information the owner did not supply, and no assumption about missing facts is stated.

rubric.name: unknown surfacing
rubric.description: Scores treatment of what the memo does not know. 2 = the memo names the specific unknowns that would change this decision (data size, residency or data-location obligations, contractual uptime terms, who operates the database day to day, traffic shape), marks which it assumed versus which need confirmation, and flags the plan elements that move if an assumption is wrong. 1 = a generic 'more discovery needed' note or an assumptions paragraph with no named unknowns. 0 = missing facts are invented and asserted as certain, or unknowns are never acknowledged.

rubric.name: cutover risk & rollback
rubric.description: Scores the risk content as an executable safety plan rather than prose. 2 = the memo names the top failure modes of its OWN recommendation (e.g. replication lag at cutover, divergence during the switch, a failed switchover with no way back), gives a concrete mitigation or rollback trigger for each, and says who decides and at what point the cutover is aborted. 1 = risks are named as labels ('downtime', 'complexity') with little or no mitigation detail. 0 = no risk section, or risks discussed only for the options not chosen.

rubric.name: factual discipline
rubric.description: Scores whether the memo only asserts what it can support. 2 = every concrete number, duration, or capability claim traces to the brief, to stated arithmetic on something the owner said, or is explicitly labeled an assumption or estimate to verify; genuine unknowns stay unknown. 1 = one or two soft invented specifics (a window length, a lag estimate) but the load-bearing claims are clean. 0 = load-bearing facts are invented and presented as certain, such as specific contract terms, database sizes, or vendor capabilities the owner never stated.

provenance.derivation: Database migration decision space (in-place major-version upgrade with a maintenance window, blue-green cutover via logical replication, staged move to a managed provider) and the withheld facts (400 GB size, three-continent residency demands, 99.9% contractual uptime, no DBA, weekend traffic trough, single aging box) derived from standard industry practice only. Trap options embedded in the brief: the managed-provider move reads as the modern default but conflicts with withheld residency facts; the maintenance window conflicts with the withheld uptime commitment. Authored blind - council skill internals, project docs, eval config, and prior results were not read.
